title: The impact of the potato in Europe

paragraphs.text: The potato was first cultivated in South America between three and seven thousand years ago, though scientists believe they may have grown wild in the continent’s mountainous west-central region as long as 13,000 years ago. Early Spanish explorers of South America, who misused the indigenous Inca word batata (sweet potato) as the name for the potato, noted the importance of the root vegetable to the Incas. The local people had learned to preserve potatoes by dehydrating and mashing them into a substance called chuñu. This could be stored for up to 10 years, providing excellent insurance against crop failures. As well as eating potatoes as a staple, the Incas used them to treat injuries.

The Spanish explorers first encountered the potato in 1532 when they arrived in Peru in search of gold, and observed the Incas eating chuñu. At the time, the Spaniards failed to realise that the potato itself was of great value, but they did gradually begin to use potatoes as basic rations on board their ships. After the arrival of the potato in Spain in 1570, a few Spanish farmers began to cultivate them on a small scale, mostly to feed livestock.

From the late 16th century, potatoes slowly spread to other European countries, but they were initially regarded with suspicion and fear. Generally considered unfit for human consumption except for the starving, even peasants refused to eat from plants that produced such ugly, misshapen root vegetables and that had come from a largely unknown land. Some even felt that the plants’ physical resemblance to plants in the poisonous nightshade family suggested that potatoes were the creation of witches or devils.

When the European diet did expand to include potatoes, not only were farmers able to produce more food, countries also gained protection against the catastrophe of a grain crop failure and periodic population declines caused by famine. Highly nutritious, potatoes also helped lessen the effects of diseases such as scurvy, tuberculosis, measles and dysentery. As well as providing starch, an essential component of the human diet, potatoes are rich in vitamin C, high in potassium and an excellent source of fibre. In fact, potatoes alone supply every vital nutrient except calcium, vitamin A and vitamin D.

In most of Europe, the upper classes saw the potato’s potential before the lower classes did, and the encouragement to begin growing potatoes came from above. In France, potatoes did not achieve widespread acceptance until the late 1700s. The peasants had remained wary, despite a 1771 report by a Parisian university testifying that the potato was not harmful, but beneficial. The people began to overcome this aversion when the potato received the royal seal of approval: King Louis XVI wore its flower in his buttonhole. King Frederick the Great of Prussia (parts of present-day Germany and Poland) saw the potato’s potential to help feed his nation. He decided to use reverse psychology to encourage his subjects to begin planting potatoes. He planted potatoes in a royal field and stationed a heavy guard to protect the field from thieves. Nearby peasants assumed that anything worth guarding was worth stealing, and so crept into the field and snatched the plants for their gardens. Of course, this was entirely in line with Frederick’s wishes.

In England, farmers and urban workers initially regarded potatoes with particular distaste. Potatoes were not commonly eaten there until the government encouraged potato cultivation for badly-needed food during the shortages that resulted from the wars of the 18th century. Historians debate whether the potato was primarily a cause or an effect of the huge population boom in industrial era England. Between 1801 and 1851, the country almost doubled in population. Prior to 1800, the English diet had consisted primarily of meat, supplemented by bread, butter and cheese. Few vegetables were consumed, most being regarded as nutritionally worthless and potentially harmful. This view began to change gradually in the late 1700s. At the same time as the populations of London, Liverpool and Manchester were rapidly increasing, potatoes were enjoying unprecedented popularity among English farmers and urban workers. The Industrial Revolution was drawing an ever-increasing percentage of the populace into crowded cities, where only the rich could afford homes with ovens. And people were working 12-16 hour days which made it difficult for them to prepare food. As a high-yielding crop that could easily be prepared on an open fire, the potato was an obvious solution to these problems. The English were beginning to acquire a taste for potatoes, as is evidenced by the vegetable’s increasing popularity in recipe books from the time. Hot potato vendors, and merchants selling fish and chips wrapped in paper, became common features of city life.

The most dramatic example of the potato’s potential to alter population patterns occurred in Ireland, where the potato had become a staple food by 1800. The Irish population doubled to eight million between 1780 and 1841. This occurred without any significant expansion of industry or reform of agricultural techniques beyond the widespread cultivation of the potato. The potato was well suited to the Irish soil and climate. Its high yields allowed the poorest farmers to produce more healthy food than they needed with scarcely any investment. In addition, as no threshing, curing or grinding was necessary, this healthy food was easy to produce. Thus, the Irish embraced the potato more passionately than anyone since the Incas.
